sections.rule: One correct option. One mark each. No negative marking.
Enter the final figure only. No marks for working.
Match every pair. Two marks each. All or nothing.

paper.stem: Which statement best explains LEADS index?
options: LEADS index: It ranks countries rather than Indian states and union territories, so it cannot guide state-level policy.
LEADS index: It is a direct count of warehouse square footage and nothing more, so a state improves its score by building sheds.
LEADS index: LEADS uses stakeholder perceptions and operating indicators to compare state logistics strengths and improvement areas and encourage policy competition.
LEADS index: A high score proves every firm in the state has low logistics cost, since the index measures realised firm outcomes.

paper.caselet: A firm has long queues between stages, excess stock, repeated handling, and customers with very different speed requirements.
paper.stem: What is the best interpretation or next step?
options: Supply-chain re-engineering: Map the full flow, expose waiting and indirect costs, segment service needs, and redesign the connected process rather than one function.
Supply-chain re-engineering: Give every segment the most expensive service level, since a uniformly high standard cannot disappoint any customer group.
Supply-chain re-engineering: Add buffer stock at every hand-off so no stage ever waits, and treat the resulting inventory as the cost of good service.
Supply-chain re-engineering: Optimise each warehouse separately against its own cost target and leave the upstream effects of those choices unexamined.

paper.stem: Which statement best explains Six supply-chain drivers?
options: Six supply-chain drivers: Facilities, inventory, transportation, information, sourcing, and pricing jointly set the balance between responsiveness and efficiency.
Six supply-chain drivers: Each driver can be optimised independently, so the best network is the sum of six separate local optima.
Six supply-chain drivers: Adding facilities always lowers both total cost and total inventory, since local stock is cheaper to hold.
Six supply-chain drivers: Transportation speed alone determines supply-chain performance, because every other driver follows the delivery schedule.

paper.caselet: A student can state what Newsvendor decision is, and now has to say why it changes the next decision.
paper.stem: Which explanation best connects Newsvendor decision to the wider subject?
options: Once Newsvendor decision has settled the choice, later evidence should not change the decision.
The economic cost of being short versus long determines which point in the uncertain demand distribution is worth covering.
Newsvendor decision works independently of the people, the constraints, and the decisions around it.
Newsvendor decision improves one local measure, so whatever happens elsewhere in the connected system no longer matters here at all.

paper.stem: Which lever separates a chase strategy from a level strategy in aggregate planning?
options: Chase varies capacity to follow demand; level holds production steady and lets inventory absorb the swings.
Chase plans over a shorter horizon than level, which is why it is used for seasonal products.
Chase is used by service firms and level by manufacturers, which is the whole of the distinction.
Chase relies on subcontracting while level relies on overtime, and neither uses inventory as a buffer.

paper.caselet: Last period's forecast was 100, actual demand was 120, and alpha is 0.25.
paper.stem: What is the best interpretation or next step?
options: Exponential smoothing: Set the next forecast to 120, because the latest actual replaces the old forecast entirely.
Exponential smoothing: Move the forecast down to 95, applying the 25% adjustment against the direction of the error.
Exponential smoothing: Keep it at 100, because smoothing averages past demand and never responds to a single period's error.
Exponential smoothing: Move the next forecast upward by 25% of the 20-unit error, giving 105.

paper.caselet: A rake cycle of 99 hours breaks down as loading 3.5 hours, idle before loading 7.5, waiting for a locomotive after loading 13, transit out 34, transit back 30, and unloading and readying about 9.75.
paper.stem: Which element is the largest single inefficiency to attack, as opposed to the largest block of time?
options: Waiting for a locomotive at 13 hours, which is detention created by the engine being reassigned elsewhere.
Unloading and readying at about 9.75 hours, which is the element most directly under the plant's control.
Idle time before loading at 7.5 hours, which is pure waiting and adds nothing to the movement.
Transit out at 34 hours, which is the largest element in the cycle and therefore the biggest prize.

paper.caselet: Secondary delivery becomes more expensive than primary line-haul and dealers require an overnight service radius.
paper.stem: What is the best interpretation or next step?
options: Stockyard location trade-off: Minimise primary line-haul distance while leaving secondary delivery cost out of the comparison entirely.
Stockyard location trade-off: Re-evaluate site locations using the changed cost structure, coverage limit, demand, and minimum throughput together.
Stockyard location trade-off: Keep the existing sites, because demand locations alone determine where a stockyard belongs.
Stockyard location trade-off: Consolidate into one large site regardless of dealer distance, since fewer sites always mean lower total network cost.

paper.stem: What does the critical ratio tell you, and what range can it take?
options: It is a share of total mismatch cost, so it always lies between 0 and 1 and sets how far up the demand distribution to order.
It is the share of expected demand that has to be met to break even, and it lies somewhere between the unit cost and the selling price.
It is the ratio of underage to overage cost, and it rises without limit as margins improve.
It is the probability that a season sells out, which is estimated from last season's actual sales.

paper.caselet: A student can state what Sales and operations planning is, and now has to say why it changes the next decision.
paper.stem: Which explanation best connects Sales and operations planning to the wider subject?
options: Sales and operations planning improves one local measure, so whatever happens elsewhere in the connected system no longer matters here at all.
Sales and operations planning works in exactly the same way independently of the people, the constraints, and the decisions that surround it.
Forecasts become decisions only when demand is reconciled with the real cost and flexibility of capacity, inventory, and service.
Once Sales and operations planning has settled the choice, later evidence should not be allowed to reopen or change the decision.

paper.caselet: A retailer promises low prices and dependable availability but keeps many premium express facilities with duplicated stock.
paper.stem: Which diagnosis is best?
options: More facilities always improve both efficiency and responsiveness at the same time, so the network is already configured correctly for any promise.
Its facilities and inventory choices may be more responsive—and costly—than the competitive promise requires, so the driver configuration lacks strategic fit.
The only useful response is to add more product variety, since a wider range is what a low-price promise needs.
Pricing and supply-chain choices are unrelated, because price is set in the market while cost is settled inside operations.

paper.caselet: A components buyer supplies two lines. Line A is a mature part with high volume and stable weekly demand. Line B is a new variant with uncertain demand and frequent design changes. The buyer wants to consolidate both onto one offshore supplier to simplify management.
paper.stem: What does tailored sourcing say about that consolidation?
options: Consolidation is right, because a single supplier operating at scale lowers unit cost on both lines and simplifies coordination for the buying team.
Move both onshore instead, since offshore sourcing is unsuitable wherever design changes are expected at all.
Keep both offshore but hold extra inventory of each, which covers the lead time without changing supplier.
Split them, because no single supplier suits every product: A fits a low-cost source and B needs a responsive one.

paper.stem: Which statement best explains Bullwhip effect?
options: Bullwhip effect: It occurs only when final consumer demand itself swings sharply, so a stable retail pattern rules the effect out.
Bullwhip effect: It is the fall in transport cost that stable ordering produces once each stage batches its shipments efficiently.
Bullwhip effect: The bullwhip effect is the amplification of order variability upstream even when end-customer demand changes only modestly.
Bullwhip effect: Upstream orders are always less variable than retail sales, because each stage smooths what it passes on.

paper.caselet: A fashion item has one buying opportunity, uncertain seasonal demand, and heavy markdowns after the season.
paper.stem: Which model fits best and why?
options: A Q review model, because replenishment can occur continuously at any point after the season starts.
Newsvendor, because a one-time uncertain order turns on shortage and leftover costs.
EOQ, because demand is constant across the year and replenishment orders repeat indefinitely.
Exponential smoothing alone, because updating the forecast directly chooses the profit-maximising order quantity.

paper.caselet: A retailer sells 8,000 units of a stable line each year. Placing an order costs ₹250 whatever its size, and holding one unit for a year costs ₹10.
paper.stem: What order quantity minimises the total of ordering and holding cost?
options: 400 units
632 units
283 units
800 units

paper.caselet: A firm sells one mature high-volume item and one volatile product with short life, high stockout cost, and frequent engineering changes.
paper.stem: What is the best interpretation or next step?
options: Tailored sourcing portfolio: Choose suppliers on landed cost alone, without weighing disruption exposure or the obsolescence risk carried by a short-life product.
Tailored sourcing portfolio: Use a low-cost source for stable volume and a faster one for the volatile item, never one cost objective for every item.

Tailored sourcing portfolio: Place both items with the longest-lead, lowest-price supplier, because a single consolidated relationship simplifies management and maximises volume leverage on unit price.
Tailored sourcing portfolio: Reserve the responsive, collaborative source for the stable commodity and leave the volatile item on the slow low-price supplier.

paper.caselet: A student can state what Cold-storage expansion is, and now has to say why it changes the next decision.
paper.stem: Which explanation best connects Cold-storage expansion to the wider subject?
options: An operating capability creates value only when local demand, logistics, and capital structure keep expensive capacity productively used.
Cold-storage expansion works independently of the people, the constraints, and the decisions around it.
Once Cold-storage expansion has settled the choice, later evidence should not be allowed to reopen or change the decision.
Cold-storage expansion improves one local measure, so whatever happens elsewhere in the connected system no longer matters here at all.

paper.stem: What are standing charges in a chartered-shipping cost build-up?
options: The demurrage that becomes payable when loading or unloading runs beyond the laytime agreed in the charter.
The cost of hiring the vessel for the period, which accrues whether or not it is moving.
The port fees charged for a berth, which are levied once per call regardless of tonnage handled.
The fixed component of the barge operating cost, prorated across the days the barges are actually worked.

paper.caselet: Retail sales move slightly, but retailer, wholesaler, and manufacturer orders show progressively larger peaks and troughs.
paper.stem: What is the best interpretation or next step?
options: Bullwhip effect: Assume consumer demand moved by the same amount, and read the manufacturer's order swings as a true demand signal.
Bullwhip effect: Add more safety stock at every stage without addressing the order distortion that created the swings.
Bullwhip effect: Diagnose amplification across incentives, batching, forecast updates and lead times, since only a shared demand signal stops it.
Bullwhip effect: Ask each stage to optimise its own profit without sharing demand data, since local accountability serves the chain best.

paper.caselet: A student can state what Akshaya Patra meal logistics is, and now has to say why it changes the next decision.
paper.stem: Which explanation best connects Akshaya Patra meal logistics to the wider subject?
options: Public service quality is completed at the recipient, so production, routing, timing, and safety must hold together end to end.
Akshaya Patra meal logistics works in exactly the same way independently of the people, the constraints, and the decisions that surround it.
Once Akshaya Patra meal logistics has settled the choice, later evidence should not be allowed to reopen or change the decision.
Akshaya Patra meal logistics improves one local measure, so whatever happens elsewhere in the connected system no longer matters here at all.

paper.caselet: A student can state what Supply-chain re-engineering is, and now has to say why it changes the next decision.
paper.stem: Which explanation best connects Supply-chain re-engineering to the wider subject?
options: Supply-chain re-engineering works independently of the people, the constraints, and the decisions around it.
Time and inventory hide between organisational boundaries; end-to-end redesign makes those costs and customer trade-offs visible.
Supply-chain re-engineering improves one local measure, so effects elsewhere in the system stop mattering.
Once Supply-chain re-engineering has settled the choice, later evidence should not change the decision.

paper.caselet: A student can state what Multimodal cost trade-off is, and now has to say why it changes the next decision.
paper.stem: Which explanation best connects Multimodal cost trade-off to the wider subject?
options: A mode changes shipment size, time, handling, and stock as well as freight; total logistics cost joins those consequences.
Multimodal cost trade-off works independently of the people, the constraints, and the decisions around it.
Once Multimodal cost trade-off has settled the choice, later evidence should not change the decision.
Multimodal cost trade-off improves one local measure, so effects elsewhere in the system stop mattering.

paper.caselet: A plant needs monthly despatch to rise from 52,000 tons to 70,000. Three routes are on the table: redesign wagons to carry more per trip, add rakes to make more trips, or cut the 99-hour rake cycle so the existing rakes make more trips.
paper.stem: Why is the third route the one to take first?
options: Because railway agreements are easier to obtain than rolling stock, which makes it the fastest route to implement.
Because wagon redesign and extra rakes both raise fixed cost, and fixed cost is always the wrong lever in logistics whatever the throughput target.
Because it is the only route that increases throughput, the first two merely moving the same tonnage differently.
Because all of the extra throughput is already inside the existing cycle as waiting time, and the other two need capital and fresh stock.

paper.stem: Which statement best explains Ports and PPP?
options: Ports and PPP: Port performance is determined only by whether the terminal is publicly or privately owned, and nothing else moves the number.
Ports and PPP: Container traffic can move at scale without hinterland links, because a terminal's own handling capacity sets its throughput by itself.

Ports and PPP: Ports support trade and coastal movement; public-private participation can add capacity and operating capability, but performance still depends on connected infrastructure and governance.
Ports and PPP: Private participation automatically removes every maritime constraint, so oversight of service performance can be withdrawn once the investment arrives and the equipment is installed.

paper.caselet: A student can state what Bullwhip effect is, and now has to say why it changes the next decision.
paper.stem: Which explanation best connects Bullwhip effect to the wider subject?
options: Once Bullwhip effect has settled the choice, later evidence should not be allowed to reopen or change the decision.
Bullwhip effect improves one local measure, so whatever happens elsewhere in the connected system no longer matters here at all.
Small local reactions compound across stages; coordination and shared demand signals stop defensive decisions from amplifying uncertainty.
Bullwhip effect works in exactly the same way independently of the people, the constraints, and the decisions that surround it.

paper.caselet: A student can state what Strategic fit is, and now has to say why it changes the next decision.
paper.stem: Which explanation best connects Strategic fit to the wider subject?
options: The customer promise creates operating requirements; performance fails when the network is built for a different promise.
Strategic fit improves one local measure, so effects elsewhere in the system stop mattering.
Strategic fit works independently of the people, the constraints, and the decisions around it.
Once Strategic fit has settled the choice, later evidence should not change the decision.

paper.caselet: A central kitchen meets cooking targets, but unlabeled containers and poorly sequenced loading cause late and incorrect school deliveries.
paper.stem: What is the best interpretation or next step?
options: Akshaya Patra meal logistics: Integrate route packaging, loading order, capacity, meal windows and safety with production, which must all hold end to end.
Akshaya Patra meal logistics: Measure success only at the kitchen exit, treating everything after despatch as somebody else's responsibility.
Akshaya Patra meal logistics: Cook more food without changing dispatch, on the view that shortfalls at school are a production problem.
Akshaya Patra meal logistics: Remove menu and school identifiers from containers to speed up packing at the kitchen.

paper.caselet: A state ranks poorly on tracking, infrastructure, regulatory environment, and cargo safety in stakeholder surveys.
paper.stem: What is the best interpretation or next step?
options: LEADS index: Ignore the stakeholder evidence entirely, since perception surveys cannot indicate anything about how a state's logistics actually performs.
LEADS index: Treat the state's rank as a firm-level profit statement and plan individual company budgets from it.
LEADS index: Improve only warehouse capacity, because infrastructure, regulation, tracking, and cargo safety are not what the index reads.
LEADS index: Use the dimensions to target state policy, remembering the measure is perception-based and never a guarantee of firm performance.

paper.stem: Why is geographical diversification treated as more than a way of reaching new demand in this sector?
options: Because a larger footprint qualifies an operator for central subsidies that a single-city operator cannot claim.
Because spreading sites lowers the equity share needed, since lenders price a diversified borrower differently.
Because it reduces business risk, in an industry with seasonal demand patterns and volatile profitability.
Because operating in several states removes the exposure to electricity costs that closed competing facilities.

paper.stem: Which statement best explains Exponential smoothing?
options: Exponential smoothing: The next forecast moves opposite to the latest error, so demand running above forecast pulls the following period's forecast down.
Exponential smoothing: It discards the old forecast entirely and sets the next forecast to the latest actual demand, so history carries no weight.
Exponential smoothing: A larger alpha always produces a smoother and slower response, because alpha measures how much of the old forecast is retained.
Exponential smoothing: Exponential smoothing updates the old forecast by a fraction alpha of the latest forecast error; a larger alpha reacts more strongly to recent demand.

paper.stem: Which statement best explains Cold-storage expansion?
options: Cold-storage expansion: Debt structure and seasonal demand do not affect expansion risk once the facility is technically sound and well run.
Cold-storage expansion: A profitable existing site proves any new geography will work, because the operating model travels with the operator.
Cold-storage expansion: Cold-storage expansion must be judged through seasonal utilisation, commodity flows, operating cost, financing, and market relationships—not capacity alone.
Cold-storage expansion: Cold storage earns the same return at every utilisation level, since its costs rise and fall with the volume stored.

paper.caselet: A student can state what Ports and PPP is, and now has to say why it changes the next decision.
paper.stem: Which explanation best connects Ports and PPP to the wider subject?
options: Once Ports and PPP has settled the choice, later evidence should not change the decision.
Ports and PPP improves one local measure, so whatever happens elsewhere in the connected system no longer matters here at all.
Ports and PPP works independently of the people, the constraints, and the decisions around it.
A port is a transfer node, so capacity creates trade value only when sea-side operations and inland flows work together.

paper.stem: Which statement best explains Tailored sourcing portfolio?
options: Tailored sourcing portfolio: Innovative products with short lives must always be sourced fully offshore, since low labour cost matters most where margins are thin.

Tailored sourcing portfolio: A sourcing portfolio matches responsive sources to volatile, high-value or time-sensitive items and efficient sources to stable, predictable volume while managing disruption risk.
Tailored sourcing portfolio: Nearshoring removes every cost and disruption trade-off at once, so a closer supplier needs no comparison against a cheaper distant one on total cost.
Tailored sourcing portfolio: One globally cheapest supplier is best for every item, because unit price is the only sourcing dimension that reaches the income statement.

paper.caselet: A student can state what Transport turnaround is, and now has to say why it changes the next decision.
paper.stem: Which explanation best connects Transport turnaround to the wider subject?
options: Transport turnaround works in exactly the same way independently of the people, the constraints, and the decisions that surround it.
Transport turnaround improves one local measure, so whatever happens elsewhere in the connected system no longer matters here at all.
Removing non-value waiting increases the productive cycles of the same asset, linking coordination directly to capacity.
Once Transport turnaround has settled the choice, later evidence should not be allowed to reopen or change the decision.

paper.stem: In exponential smoothing, what is the smoothing constant actually deciding?
options: How many past periods are averaged before the mean of that window is taken as the next forecast.
The width of the tolerance band inside which a forecast counts as having been accurate.
How far ahead the forecast can be projected before it must be recalculated from scratch.
The proportion of the last forecast error carried into the next forecast, so every forecast is the previous one corrected.

paper.stem: Which statement best explains Akshaya Patra meal logistics?
options: Akshaya Patra meal logistics: Cooking volume alone determines successful meal delivery, because a kitchen that meets its target has met its obligation.
Akshaya Patra meal logistics: Route labels and loading sequence have no effect on service, since every container eventually holds the same meal for the same schools.

Akshaya Patra meal logistics: Akshaya Patra coordinates menu, mechanised production, labelled containers, route sequencing, vehicles, hygiene, and school time windows as one high-volume service system.
Akshaya Patra meal logistics: Nutritional standards can be set separately from menu and logistics design, because nutrition is decided before any vehicle is loaded.

paper.stem: How does India's use of shipping compare with the global pattern?
options: India ships over 95% of its trade by volume against a global 80%, but only 65% by value against a global 70%.
India ships a smaller share of its trade by volume than the world average, but a larger share by value.
India's volume and value shares are both close to the global figures, so its port profile is unremarkable.
India ships almost all of its trade by sea on both measures at once, which is what distinguishes it from other large coastal economies.

paper.caselet: A manufacturer's order book swings violently while the retailer's consumer sales barely move. Each stage in between says it is simply ordering against what it can see, and none has changed its ordering rule.
paper.stem: What is the most defensible diagnosis?
options: Consumer demand must in fact be moving somewhere, since order swings this large cannot arise from genuinely stable end demand.
The forecasts are poor; better forecasting at each stage would remove most of the amplification.
One stage is over-ordering deliberately to protect itself, and the swings will settle once that stage has been identified.
The chain is structural: delay, partial information and local ordering rules produce this even when every stage orders rationally.

paper.caselet: A forecast rises sharply, but the plant has long training times and cheap storage.
paper.stem: What should planning do next?
options: Use the forecast directly as the production order without checking capacity, since the forecast is what the plant has committed to deliver.
Ignore inventory entirely, because forecasting and operations are separate functions that hand work to each other in sequence.
Fire and rehire workers each period regardless of training cost, because output should track demand exactly month by month.
Translate the forecast into a capacity-and-inventory plan, likely using stable capacity with inventory and limited flexibility rather than blindly chasing demand.

paper.caselet: Two customer groups buy one product. One group accepts delivery any time within a few days. The other needs it inside a narrow window each morning.
paper.stem: Which customer-profile attribute separates these two groups?
options: Order size, since a customer needing a fixed time is usually buying in smaller quantities.
Cost sensitivity, because a narrow delivery window is a premium service and is priced as one.
Reverse logistics needs, since tighter delivery windows generate more returns and repeat visits.
Timeliness, which is a separate attribute from response time and is what decides the design here.

paper.caselet: A network adds stockyards and vehicles, yet orders remain late because loaded assets wait at every organisational hand-off.
paper.stem: What should be investigated first?
options: Only the purchase price of the new vehicles, since asset cost is what the investment case turns on.
End-to-end cycle time and hand-off coordination, because idle detention can consume capacity despite more physical assets.
A larger safety-stock target at every node, because more stock at each point protects the delivery promise.
Removal of shared performance measures, so each site is judged only on what it controls directly.

paper.caselet: A student can state what Tailored sourcing portfolio is, and now has to say why it changes the next decision.
paper.stem: Which explanation best connects Tailored sourcing portfolio to the wider subject?
options: Once Tailored sourcing portfolio has settled the choice, later evidence should not be allowed to reopen or change the decision.
Tailored sourcing portfolio improves one local measure, so whatever happens elsewhere in the connected system no longer matters here at all.
Different demand and product risks require different source capabilities; a portfolio prevents one cost objective from governing every item.
Tailored sourcing portfolio works independently of the people, the constraints, and the decisions around it.

paper.caselet: A student can state what Six supply-chain drivers is, and now has to say why it changes the next decision.
paper.stem: Which explanation best connects Six supply-chain drivers to the wider subject?
options: Once Six supply-chain drivers has settled the choice, later evidence should not change the decision.
Six supply-chain drivers improves one local measure, so whatever happens elsewhere in the connected system no longer matters here at all.
Managers deliver strategic fit by configuring several connected drivers, not by maximising one lever in isolation.
Six supply-chain drivers works independently of the people, the constraints, and the decisions around it.

paper.caselet: A value retailer promises low prices and dependable availability on a stable range of staples. Its distribution runs on full truckloads, long production batches and suppliers selected mainly on landed cost. A new leadership team wants to add two-hour delivery in eight cities without changing sourcing, transport or the range.
paper.stem: What does this proposal do to the retailer's strategic fit?
options: It improves fit, since faster service is a stronger customer promise than dependable availability at a low price.
It breaks fit, because a two-hour promise raises implied uncertainty while the chain is still built for efficiency.
It leaves fit intact, because the range and the suppliers are unchanged and the promise is what customers judge.
It has no bearing on fit, which is decided by the competitive strategy on its own rather than by the chain.

paper.caselet: A student can state what Economic order quantity is, and now has to say why it changes the next decision.
paper.stem: Which explanation best connects Economic order quantity to the wider subject?
options: Economic order quantity improves one local measure, so effects elsewhere in the system stop mattering.
Economic order quantity works independently of the people, the constraints, and the decisions around it.
Once Economic order quantity has settled the choice, later evidence should not change the decision.
Lot size sets the ordering-versus-holding trade-off; reorder timing answers a different question about when replenishment must start.

paper.stem: Which statement best explains Supply-chain re-engineering?
options: Supply-chain re-engineering: It means cutting one department's budget without examining the stages upstream and downstream of it.
Supply-chain re-engineering: Re-engineering redesigns end-to-end flows to remove hidden time, inventory, hand-offs, and cost while meeting distinct customer service needs.
Supply-chain re-engineering: Customer segments should receive identical logistics regardless of need, since one uniform service level is simplest to run and audit.
Supply-chain re-engineering: More inventory is the default answer to every service problem, because stock is what protects a customer from delay.

paper.caselet: A buyer places one pre-season order for a printed festive range. Demand for the print is uncertain, there is no chance to reorder once the season starts, and unsold stock is cleared at well below cost afterwards.
paper.stem: Which model does this description specify, and which clause settles it?
options: Aggregate planning, settled by the seasonal pattern, which is what a chase, flexibility or level strategy is chosen against each season.
Exponential smoothing, settled by the uncertainty in demand, which is what a forecast exists to handle.
Economic order quantity, settled by the fact that stock is being ordered in a batch rather than continuously.
The newsvendor model, settled by there being one buying opportunity with no replenishment and a salvage value below cost.

paper.caselet: A network study finds that removing the secondary-distance limit gives the lowest total cost of any scenario. Overnight service to dealers requires secondary movement to stay inside 350 kilometres.
paper.stem: What follows for the recommendation?
options: The service promise should be dropped, because the model has shown the constraint to be expensive.
The 350-kilometre solution should be adopted and its extra cost read as the price of the overnight promise.
The unconstrained solution should be adopted, since it is the lowest total cost the model was able to find.
The two results should be averaged, since the true optimum must lie somewhere between an unconstrained and a constrained run.

paper.caselet: Sea transport lands a year's ore far below the rail cost, but moves the whole quantity in one or two shipments and therefore holds far more inventory. Several other options sit between the two on both counts.
paper.stem: How should the inventory carrying cost be brought into the comparison?
options: Compute it for every option, since a ranking cannot be trusted until each of them has been costed on the same basis over the same period.
Compute it only for the option holding the most inventory: if even that still wins, no other option can overturn the ranking.
Leave it out, because carrying cost is an accounting charge rather than a cash cost of moving the material.
Apply a standard percentage to each option's transport cost, which keeps the comparison consistent across modes.

paper.caselet: Ahead of the festive season a packaged food brand's marketing team plans a large promotion, operations plans stable production to avoid overtime, procurement plans a bulk packaging buy, and finance plans to hold working capital down. Each plan is signed off inside its own function.
paper.stem: What is the failure this situation describes?
options: One of the four functions has misread the demand forecast, and the other three are correct exactly as they stand.
Every function is right on its own terms, and the firm has four defensible plans where it needs one agreed plan.
The promotion should be cancelled, because a supply chain cannot support a demand spike it did not create.
Working capital targets should always outrank promotional plans, since inventory is the most expensive buffer.

paper.caselet: A regional warehouse forecast 1,200 units for last month. Actual demand came in at 1,320 units. The smoothing constant in use is 0.2.
paper.stem: A regional warehouse forecast 1,200 units for last month. Actual demand came in at 1,320 units. The smoothing constant in use is 0.2.
paper.prompt: What is the forecast for this month?

paper.caselet: A distributor settles on an order quantity of 600 units against annual demand of 12,000 units, an ordering cost of ₹600 per order, and a holding cost of ₹40 per unit per year.
paper.stem: A distributor settles on an order quantity of 600 units against annual demand of 12,000 units, an ordering cost of ₹600 per order, and a holding cost of ₹40 per unit per year.
paper.prompt: What is the total annual ordering plus holding cost at that order quantity?

paper.caselet: A seasonal item sells for ₹900 and costs ₹500 to buy. There is one buying opportunity, and anything unsold at the end of the season clears at ₹200.
paper.stem: A seasonal item sells for ₹900 and costs ₹500 to buy. There is one buying opportunity, and anything unsold at the end of the season clears at ₹200.
paper.prompt: What is the critical ratio? Give it as a decimal.

paper.caselet: A distributor expects steady annual demand of 12,000 units. Each order placed costs ₹600 regardless of its size. Holding one unit for a year costs ₹40.
paper.stem: A distributor expects steady annual demand of 12,000 units. Each order placed costs ₹600 regardless of its size. Holding one unit for a year costs ₹40.
paper.prompt: What order quantity minimises the total of ordering and holding cost?

paper.stem: Match each prompt to the precise explanation or action.
choices: Move the next forecast upward by 25% of the 20-unit error, giving 105.
Exponential smoothing updates the old forecast by a fraction alpha of the latest forecast error; a larger alpha reacts more strongly to recent demand.
Use a level plan and draw inventory down, since a forecast becomes a decision only when reconciled with capacity cost.
S&OP balances forecast demand with capacity, utilisation, inventory, backlog, and outsourcing over a medium-term horizon.

paper.stem: Match each prompt to the precise explanation or action.
choices: A sourcing portfolio matches responsive sources to volatile, high-value or time-sensitive items and efficient sources to stable, predictable volume while managing disruption risk.
Use a low-cost source for stable volume and a faster one for the volatile item, never one cost objective for every item.
The bullwhip effect is the amplification of order variability upstream even when end-customer demand changes only modestly.
